title: Caught in the Squall
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] I'd been fishing that same stretch of coastline since childhood, which is probably why I ignored the warning signs longer than I should have.
Narrator: The sky had turned a strange greenish grey an hour earlier, but I told myself, as fishermen often do, that it would blow over.
Narrator: [carefully] It didn't blow over. Within twenty minutes, the wind had doubled, and waves that had been gentle were suddenly slamming against the hull.
Narrator: I remember gripping the wheel so tightly my knuckles ached, calculating whether I could outrun the squall or whether I'd simply exhaust the engine trying.
Narrator: [reflective] Strangely, what I recall most clearly isn't fear itself, but how quiet my thinking became, as though panic had been switched off to make room for something more useful.
Narrator: Every instinct I'd absorbed from my father over decades surfaced automatically, turning the bow into the waves rather than letting them strike side-on.
Narrator: [honestly] Had I turned broadside even once, the boat would almost certainly have capsized, given how violently the swells were building by then.
Narrator: For nearly forty minutes, I fought that sea with no real sense of whether I was gaining ground or merely surviving the current wave before the next arrived.
Narrator: [gently] Eventually, the wind eased, not gradually but almost abruptly, the way storms sometimes exhaust themselves without any warning at all.
Narrator: I sat there afterward, soaked and shaking, staring at a sea that had gone nearly calm, as if it hadn't just tried to swallow me whole.
Narrator: [calmly] What stayed with me wasn't pride at having survived, but a renewed humility, the reminder that the ocean tolerates us rather than welcomes us.
Narrator: These days, I still fish that coastline, but I no longer dismiss a greenish sky as mere coincidence, and I've never once regretted turning back early since.
